title: Jazz Information and a white audience that cared
summary: Hodes describes the New York jazz movement of Columbia kids, Milt Gabler and Commodore records. He contrasts the Chicago white audience, who liked Wayne King.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: There was a magazine called Jazz Information, and I was enthralled with this, that there was people that were so crazy about this music. Because that never happened in Chicago. The only -- you see, the blacks had their people to play for, but the whites didn't have it. The white audience was the Wayne King audience, what we have now, the Lawrence Welk audience, is what we had then, in the Wayne King audience.

If you played jazz, you were persona non grata. And if you played your music at night on that Victrola, you better turn it down real soft, and even use a pin for a needle, because if it got too loud, the neighbors would call the law, that noise, they couldn't stand that noise.
